L01: The town of Alderly had three churches, two pubs, and one secret that everyone knew but no one spoke about out loud. The churches were old and cold and smelled of damp hymnals. The pubs were warm and loud and smelled of everything else. The secret — well, the secret smelled of the sea, even though the sea was forty miles away, which was part of what made it strange. Margaret Holt had lived on the high street for sixty-two years. She had watched the elm trees grow and die and be replaced with saplings that were now, themselves, beginning to look like trees. She had watched the post office become a letting agency and the letting agency become a coffee shop and the coffee shop become, briefly, a yoga studio before it became a coffee shop again. She had watched the secret pulse through the town like a second heartbeat, quiet but constant, something the young people thought they'd discovered and the old people knew had always been there. Her granddaughter Rosie had come to visit for the summer, which was part of why Margaret was sitting now at the kitchen window, watching the garden and waiting. Rosie was seventeen and curious in the way that seventeen always is — not curious about answers, but about the questions themselves, which is a kind of courage Margaret had spent decades trying to relearn.
L02: Chapter Four: The Last Map. There is a map in the British Library that is wrong in a way that can only be described as deliberately wrong. It was drawn in 1602 by a cartographer whose name has been lost, which is itself suspicious, since cartographers of that period were meticulous about attribution. The map shows the eastern coast of an island that does not exist. The island is rendered in extraordinary detail — bays, inlets, a river that curves south before turning back on itself, a mountain with a notation in Latin that translates, roughly, as 'here the light is different.' On the reverse side of the map, in a hand that appears to be different from the cartographer's, someone has written: 'I have been here.' Dr. Evelyn Cross had been studying this map for eleven years. She had examined it under ultraviolet light, under infrared imaging, under a microscope powerful enough to count the individual fibres of the vellum. She had traced the coastline against every known island in every ocean and found nothing. She had run the Latin text through six different translation tools and received six slightly different answers, all of which agreed on 'light' and disagreed on everything else. Today, for reasons she couldn't fully explain, she thought she was close.
L03: Good evening. I'm Sarah Chen, and this is the 6 o'clock news. Our top story tonight: the government has announced an emergency package worth 14 billion pounds to help households and businesses with rising energy costs. The Chancellor confirmed the measures in a statement to Parliament this afternoon, saying the package would take effect from the 1st of May. Under the plan, households will receive a flat payment of 400 pounds, with additional support for the lowest-income families of up to 650 pounds. Businesses in the hospitality, retail, and manufacturing sectors will receive rebates on their energy bills for a period of six months. The announcement was welcomed by opposition leaders, though the shadow chancellor called it too little too late, pointing out that average household bills have risen by 67 percent over the past 18 months. Industry groups broadly welcomed the support but said longer-term solutions were still needed. The cost of the package will be funded partly through a windfall tax on energy companies, which the government is extending for a further two years. Several energy firms said they would review planned investment in domestic production following the announcement. We'll have more on this story throughout the evening. Now let's go to our economics correspondent James Okafor, who is outside the Treasury.
L04: Lesson 4: Understanding the Water Cycle. Water is constantly moving around our planet in a cycle — from the surface up into the atmosphere and back down again. This is called the water cycle, or the hydrological cycle, and it has been happening for billions of years. Let's start with evaporation. When the sun heats water in oceans, lakes, and rivers, some of that water turns into water vapour — a gas — and rises into the air. Oceans are the main source of evaporated water, which makes sense when you think about how much of the Earth's surface they cover. As the water vapour rises, it enters cooler parts of the atmosphere. When warm, moist air cools down, the water vapour condenses — meaning it turns back into tiny liquid droplets. These droplets collect together to form clouds. You might have noticed that clouds often form at a certain altitude — that's because that's the point where the rising air has cooled just enough for condensation to begin. When enough droplets collect in a cloud, they become too heavy to stay suspended in the air, and they fall as precipitation — which is rain, snow, sleet, or hail depending on the temperature. Some of this precipitation flows into rivers and streams and eventually back to the sea. Some of it soaks into the ground and becomes groundwater. And some of it falls as snow on high mountains and stays frozen for months or even years before slowly melting. And then the whole cycle begins again. Every glass of water you drink has been through this cycle countless times.

L08: There is a village in the western Highlands where the shore road ends at a cattle grid, and beyond the cattle grid there is only heather, sea, and the sound of curlews. The village is called Applecross, though on the older maps and in the older Gaelic it was A' Chomraich — meaning the sanctuary. In the eighth century a monk called Maelrubha came here from Bangor and founded a monastery whose stones lie now under the churchyard grass. What he built was more than a monastery. It was a place of refuge, marked by four crosses at the compass points, and any fugitive who reached them, whatever the crime, could not be pursued within their circle. This right of sanctuary held for a thousand years, and was still recognised into the seventeenth century, when Highland courts continued to acknowledge the boundary even as they otherwise wielded a punishing law. Today the crosses are gone, or perhaps buried, and the road ends where the road ends. But in the way that certain landscapes hold memory in their weather — the sudden hush that falls when you turn the last bend, the sense that the light has changed in some quiet, deliberate way — something of the sanctuary is still there, waiting for the traveller who thinks they have arrived, and finds instead that they have been received.
